Anthropic's Frontier Red Team believes small AI models may now be months away from being capable of self replicating without access to a datacenter.

Quoting from the blog:

'The capabilities that make AI models generally powerful coding agents also generalize to cyber tasks, including autonomous replication. Like coding agents in 2024, we’re seeing signs of life for AI worms. We don’t yet have a full rogue replicator, but agents are becoming increasingly capable of completing the individual steps in the replication chain (and passing on their adaptations to future copies of themselves).

At the same time, increasing amounts of inference compute are now available both inside and outside of datacenters (see Appendix D). It’s uncertain exactly what form autonomous AI replication will take. It could be a slow, distributed “digital slime mold,” living on relatively insecure compute. It could also be a powerful cyber model that breaches datacenters at a high pace, or a model that scams people for compute credits.

As a prediction that goes beyond our experiments, we expect a future awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren’t under human control. While it’s true that IoT devices have been vulnerable for a long time, lightweight agents may be much more willing than human attackers to put in the effort to compromise large fractions of the world’s IoT compute. The rise of slow replicators would also be a bellwether for more aggressive, faster ones that can breach more hardened machines or be effective API key thieves. We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay.'

We don’t yet have a full rogue replicator, but agents are becoming increasingly capable of completing the individual steps in the replication chain (and passing on their adaptations to future copies of themselves).

At the same time, increasing amounts of inference compute are now available both inside and outside of datacenters (see Appendix D). It’s uncertain exactly what form autonomous AI replication will take. It could be a slow, distributed “digital slime mold,” living on relatively insecure compute. It could also be a powerful cyber model that breaches datacenters at a high pace, or a model that scams people for compute credits.

As a prediction that goes beyond our experiments, we expect a future awash with agents running on all types of hardware, including some that aren’t under human control. While it’s true that IoT devices have been vulnerable for a long time, lightweight agents may be much more willing than human attackers to put in the effort to compromise large fractions of the world’s IoT compute. The rise of slow replicators would also be a bellwether for more aggressive, faster ones that can breach more hardened machines or be effective API key thieves. We should aim to harden our systems to make it difficult for such replicators to spread, but also prepare to deal with a world where they are here to stay.'

All this reverse engineering and cracking of software/video games because of AI has me very worried and I believe will lead to fewer freedoms, not more.

Companies now have zero incentive to ship you a binary without extreme DRM and hardware level anti-consumer sniffers and telemetry.

Reverse engineering copyright was always a very grey area because of how difficult and painstaking it was. Now with AI, one person can crack a game in weeks, not years and years needing a whole team.

This will likely lead to companies justifying ending client based software delivery in favor of streaming based cloud services and games.

At its very worst, consumer hardware and GPUs with local AI may get classified as “pirating machines” that become difficult or illegal to own because of how copyright and ownership laws get re-written around AI.

It’s not “you will own nothing and be happy” it’s “you will stream everything off a server and be complacent”.

RT @0xJohannes_: UPDATE: I can confirm that the Ledger supply chain is compromised in Europe as well. @Ledger should initiate an immediate product recall to protect users.

I just purchased a second device from a different Mediamarkt location today, recorded the unboxing process, and discovered spyware once again (video linked in the second tweet).

The device was compromised in the exact same manner, featuring identical modifications (such as additional cables and an LTE module). This indicates its a widespread issue rather than an isolated incident, potentially affecting Ledger inventory across MediaMarkt and Saturn stores throughout Europe (comprising over 1,000 stores across 11 countries).

My initial hypothesis was that these devices were returns that looked unopened to the employees and were just sold again as new however, a MediaMarkt employee confirmed that the device I purchased was not a return, and that returned Ledgers are sent directly back to the manufacturer rather than resold.

Store records show the inventory originated from Aqipa GmbH. While Ledger's CTO was unsure if Aqipa serves as the direct distributor between Ledger and MediaMarkt, it appears to be the case. Given that Aqipa distributes across Europe, any physical retail store receiving stock through them may be at risk.

I sent the first ledger to mark and the second one is going to ledger now, so that they can analyse it.
If you purchased a ledger from anyone other than the official ledger store, make sure to check your device!!

RT @aakashgupta: Walmart is selling real diamond earrings for $12.

Not a typo. Half-carat lab-grown diamonds, same carbon, graded by the same labs that grade the stone in your engagement ring. A jeweler can't tell them apart without a machine.

And that $12 price tag is why the company that invented the engagement ring is about to get sold for scrap.

De Beers ran the diamond trade for over a century. At its peak it controlled up to 90% of the world's rough supply, and when demand dipped it just locked diamonds in London vaults until prices came back. The slogan "A Diamond Is Forever" came from their ad agency in 1947. So did the rule that a ring should cost two months of your salary. Before that campaign, most American brides never got a diamond at all.

The whole thing held for 80 years because there were only so many mines. Then China started growing diamonds in reactors, and there's no vault on earth big enough to hide a factory's output.

Lab-grown wholesale prices have crashed roughly 96% from their peak, down to around $100 a carat. The Knot says 61% of engagement rings sold in 2025 had lab-grown center stones, up 239% since 2020. Even De Beers' own average selling price fell 32% in a year, to $105 a carat.

So Anglo American, which owns De Beers, has written it down by $6.8 billion in two years and is now in talks to sell the whole thing for about $1 billion. This is a company that was valued over $18 billion in 2001 and $13 billion as recently as 2011.

The stones coming out of the ground are the same as ever. The only scarce thing De Beers ever owned was the marketing, and marketing doesn't survive a $12 price tag at Walmart.

Honestly bro, if you really want to learn about goop, I'd recommend just reading over MITRE ATT&CK.

MITRE ATT&CK basically documents known attacker techniques (especially in regards to malware). I think it's a good starting point because it introduces you to goop theory rather than diving directly into the trenches of malware code.

If you don't know what goop can do, then you won't have any idea what the goop is trying to accomplish. If you understand what goop can do, will do, or wants to accomplish, writing goop or reverse engineering goop is substantially easier.

Skim through MITRE ATT&CK, see if anything sticks out and seems interesting, and read it. If you don't understand it, ask Mr. AI what it means and unironically have a conversation with Mr. AI about what it means and how it works.

If you think it's boring, or still too complicated, stop reading it. Goop is supposed to be fun. If you're bored from it, or if it still seems too complicated, you might not be ready for that particular set of information, and that's okay.

When you read about the goop, you should be so excited by how cool it is, you should want to call your Mom on the phone and tell her all about it (she's a nice lady, she'll listen and support you).

Additionally, submerge yourself in the goop. Let it engulf you. Pay attention to what companies are doing write-ups on goop (there's a lot, actually), pay attention to what people online say about the goop. Live, laugh, and love the goop.

I unironically think there is like, a brain goop muscle or something, because at first it'll be kind of hard. You will struggle with the goop. But, if you're consistent, like an hour a day or something, then eventually that hour will feel like 10 minutes and you'll find yourself wanting to do more goop.

I've been doing malware stuff for over 20 years. Writing malware and reverse engineering malware doesn't feel like a chore or task, it feels like ... almost like what some people describe as watching movies or playing video games. It's extremely fun, entertaining, engaging, and I look forward everyday to doing it. I can lock in for hours and not even be remotely bored.

However, if you're new to goop it will not be this way. Your goop muscles are soft and weak. They're not prepared. You have to strengthen them first.

Okay, I hope that answers some of the DMs you stinky ass nerds have sent me. I love you. Toodles

tweets.content:
Defense has fundamentally shifted away from an external actor/campaign-centric model toward insider threat, but so much of what we’ve built over the past 15+ years wasn’t designed for this. Years of ATT&CK bingo have atrophied the muscles required to combat subtle acts of subversion, and now they’re occurring at machine speed and often without the users’ knowledge.

Countless teams I talk with are drowning in alerts generated by agents operating in massive grey areas, doing things that look malicious but are completely benign and vice versa. The missing piece is, as it always has been, the intent behind the action. False positive tuning was already the painful exercise of explaining that intent in org-specific context so we could make exceptions for acceptable behavior. Agents make that substantially harder through their speed, volume, and contextual ambiguity.

The next generation of security controls has to reason about intent in organizational context, because the behaviors we’ve spent many years learning to detect are becoming indistinguishable from the work we’re paying agents to do.
